bayou-vidal-bayou-vidal-1900-08-04.A1:
NEW STYLE OF LYNCHING.
A NEGRO TORTURED INTO CONFESSION. SEWED UP IN A SACK. WEIGHTED AND DROPPED OVERBOARD.
AND DROPPED OVERBOARD.

New-Orleans, Aug. 4 (Special).—News has just reached this city from Bayou Vidal, La., of a negro lynching at that place with some few variations from the accustomed formula. An old farmer of the neighborhood was murdered last week, and his body sunk in the Bayou, the object being robbery. A strange negro, seen wandering in the neighborhood, was suspected of the crime and put to torture to force a confession. A chain, the same he had used in weighing down the body, was fastened about the colored man's waist, and he was repeatedly sunk in the Bayou, being hauled out before death resulted. At last the negro gave up, and acknowledged the crime. Thereupon he was forced into a sack, which was sewed up, heavily weighted and dropped into the water at the place where his victim had been found.
bayou-vidal-bayou-vidal-1900-08-04.A2:
DROWNED HIM LIKE A BEAST.
Whites Sewed a Negro in a Sack, Weight Him
and Throw Him Into the Bayon.
NEW ORLEANS Aug A—A few days ago.
NEW ORLEANS, Aug. 4. A few days ago a white farmer living in Bayou Vidal in Concordia parish, La., was murdered and the body sunk in the bayou with stones attached. The people of the neighborhood suspected a negro of the name of Scott of the crime. To-day Scott was arrested and taken to the scene of the murder. He was weighted with chains and thrown into the bayou, but dragged out just before he drowned. This was repeated several times when Scott confessed to the murder. He was then sewed in a sack, weighted with stones and thrown into the bayou, where he sunk out of sight.
bayou-vidal-bayou-vidal-1900-08-04.A3:
PUNISHED BY DROWNING.
Negro Sewed in a Sack and Thrown Into a Bayou.
NEW ORLEANS, Aug. 5.—A few days ago a white farmer living in Bayou Vidal, in Concordia Parish, was murdered and the body sunk in the bayou with stones attached. The people of the neighborhood suspected a strange negro named Scott of the crime. Yesterday Scott was arrested and taken to the scene of the murder. He was weighted with chains and thrown into the bayou, but dragged out just before he drowned. This was repeated several times, when Scott confessed to the murder. He was then sewed in a sack, weighted with stones, and thrown into the bayou, where he sunk out of sight.

bibbs-huntsville-1900-08-14.A1:
BIG MOB AFTER
ANOTHER NEGRO

Assaulted White Woman in Ten-
nessee and Fled into Mad-
ison County, Ala.
Huntsville, August 9.—(Special.)—Mrs. Alonzo Gillham, wife of a prominent young planter of Lincoln County, Tennessee, was criminally assaulted by a negro this afternoon at her home near Lincoln post office. Mrs. Gillham was called to the door and a negro confronted her. She asked him what he wanted and he replied that he wanted her. He then assaulted Mrs. Gillham, who resisted with almost superhuman strength and the negro lost his courage and fled. The woman was found in an unconscious condition.

A mob was formed and has followed the negro across the State line into Madison County, Alabama. Hounds have been sent for. Mrs. Gillman is connected with leading families of Fayetteville, Tenn., and a number of men of that place are in the mob.
bibbs-huntsville-1900-08-14.A6:
MOB'S FRUITLESS SEARCH
Scoured Lincoln and Madison Counties All During the Day
Huntsville, August 10.—(Special.)—The Lincoln County mob today has scoured Lincoln and Madison Counties for the assailant of Mrs. Alonzo Gillham. Jim Scott, colored, was captured north of Gurley, but he proved to be the wrong man and was turned loose. Deputy Sheriff Johnston of Chattanooga reached the scene of the crime this morning with the Phipps bloodhounds, but the dogs would not work, as the scent was cold. Private citizens have offered offered a reward of several hundred dollars for the capture of the negro, and Governor McMillan has been requested to offer one.
bibbs-huntsville-1900-08-14.A8:
MOB HAS A NEGRO
They Think He Committed the Assault on Mrs. Gillham
Huntsville, August 13.—(Special.)—A determined band of men who have been in Madison county several days looking for the assailant of Mrs. Alonzo Gillham at Lincoln, Tenn., have captured a negro near Fort Deposit who exactly corresponds with Mrs. Gillham's description of her assailant. The negro will be hustled up to Mrs. Gillham for identification.
bibbs-huntsville-1900-08-14.A10: The negro carried from this place last night to Lincoln, Tenn., by a determined mob of Lincoln County citizens was today carried before Mrs. Gillham and positively identified as her assailant. The negro positively identified in his former statements that he was at work for State Senator Ed L. Pulley, at his summer home home on Monte Sano, on the day the crime is alleged to have been committed. The mob is composed of the best citizens of Lincoln County, and not wishing to punish any but but the guilty party, they consented to await the arrival party, they consented to await the arrival of Senator Pulley, by whom the negro proposed to prove an alibi.
bibbs-huntsville-1900-08-14.A12:
QUESTION OF IDENTITY Is All That Is Saving a Negro From the Fury of a Tennessee Mob.
Fayetteville, Tenn., Aug. 14.—[Special.]—The negro brought here from Huntsville last night by a mob of angry Lincoln county citizens was to-day carried before Mrs. Gilham and identified as her assailant.

The negro persisted in his former statements that he was at work for State Senator Ed L. Pulley, at his summer home on Mount Zano, on the day the crime is alleged to have been committed.

The mob did not want to punish any but the guilty man, and consented to await the arrival of Senator Pulley, by whom the negro proposed to prove an alibi. Upon his arrival Mr. Pulley identified the negro as one who had worked for him on the day of the crime, and addressed a communication to Mrs. Gilham, tending to show that he was in Alabama on that day.

Mrs. Gilham then addressed a letter to the mob, in which she expressed some doubt as to Gibbs being the right man. This letter was read to them by her father. The husband of Mrs. Gilham also counseled the mob to be careful and prudent.

A committee was appointed to investigate the alibi proven, and the negro was placed in the Lincoln county jail under promise of his captors that he would be turned over to the people to be hanged if proven guilty.

A delegation left Fayetteville to-night for Huntsville to investigate the matter.

Nashville, Tenn., Aug. 16.—[Special.] Tom Bibb, the alleged assailant of Mrs. Gillham, of Lincoln county, was brought to Nashville from Fayetteville this morning and lodged in jail. Fear of mob violence at Fayetteville caused the negro's removal to this city.
bibbs-huntsville-1900-08-14.A14:
Still Getting Evidence
Huntsville, Aug. 17.—(Special.)—The committee appointed by the people of Lincoln county to ascertain the guilt of Tom Bibb, charged with an assault upon Mrs. Alonzo Gillham, is still in Madison County collecting evidence. The result of their research has not been announced.

The committee was non-plussed by the removal of Bibb to the Nashville jail, and it is hardly probable that any further steps will be taken by the mob.
bibbs-huntsville-1900-08-14.A16:
MOB DISAPPOINTED.
The Alleged Assailant of Mrs. Gilliam Secure In Nashville Jail.
A Huntsville, Ala., dispatch says: Sheriff H. R. Melson, of Lincoln county, Tennessee, has hustled Tom Bibbs, the suspected assailant of Mrs. Alonzo Gilliam, of Lincoln, Tenn., from Favetteville to the jail in Nashville for safe keeping.

Further rumors of a mob caused the officer to take the precaution, but in doing so he is the object of criticism, as he promised the mob that he would not remove the prisoner from the Fayetteville jail under any circumstances, but of course, this was an illegal promise on the part of the officer.

The representatives of the Tennessee mob, who had been in Huntsville and other places, began to return to their homes after investigating the history of Tom Bibbs.

It was finally announced that the committee had secured sufficient proof that Bibbs is the right negro. They gave the negro the benefit of every doubt, and also allowed Senator Pulley and others to try and prove an alibi for him, but so far they have failed, and members of the mob, with the information they are working on and what they had, are convinced that they have the right man, and despite the fact that the prisoner has been carried to Nashville, when they conclude their investigation, they say, they will get their man.

RICHARDSON To Move Democratic Congressional Headquarters TO NEW YORK CITY. WILL FACILITATE WORK WITH THE NATIONAL COMMITTEE.
Washington, Aug. 27.—[Special.]—Representative Richardson, chairman of the Democratic Congressional Committee, to-day announced that he would remove his headquarters to New York and would in the future be associated with Gov. W. J. Stone, vice chairman of the Democratic National Committee; Senator Gorman and National Committeeman Guffy, of Pennsylvania; Mack, of New York, and Campau, of Michigan, in the management of the campaign in the East. This arrangement brings the Congressional Committee in closer touch with the National Committee, and facilitates the work of both bodies. The headquarters here will be maintained under the management of Secretary Kerr, who as heretofore will direct the distribution of the majority of the literature used in the campaign. Representative Richardson expects to leave to-morrow for New York.

Representative Gilbert and others in Kentucky have recently appealed to the committee for copies of Mr. Justice Brown's speech against the imperialistic tendencies of McKinley's Administration. The speech is one of the ablest efforts on the subject, and in response to the numerous requests the committee have decided to print one million copies for distribution. The committee sent out last week through the mails nearly 2,000,000 documents.

RACE RIOT NARROWLY AVERTED.
New Orleans Police Save a Negro From a Mob.
New Orleans Police Save a Negro From a Mob.

CHICAGO, August 17.—A special to the Tribune from New Orleans says:

Another outbreak against the negroes was narrowly averted here last night. Branch Payne, a powerful negro, living in the neighborhood in which Robert Charles, the negro desperado, was killed a few weeks ago, opened fire on two deputy sheriffs who attempted to arrest him on a warrant charging shooting at a white man.

The negro resisted arrest and shot at the officers, who returned the fire. Four shots were exchanged. Angry citizens quickly gathered, but the police charged the crowd in numbers and forced a dispersal.

The negro, frightened by the demonstration, submitted peacefully to arrest and is now in jail with double guards protecting him.

dock-thomas-chicago-1900-08.A1:
Rescued by Police.
A crowd of nearly a hundred infuriated men and boys chased "Dock" Thomas, a colored Pullman car porter, off the dock into the lake at Chicago, and but for the timely arrival of the police would probably have stoned him to death in the water. Thomas and another colored man were fishing and became involved in a quarrel. They hurled stones at each other, one of which struck a woman on the head. Then the crowd ran after Thomas yelling "kill him," finally forcing him into the water. A perfect hail of stones then fell around him, but before he was seriously injured the police arrived.

joseph-parker-richmond-1900-07.A1:
TWO MORE HEAVY SUITS Filed Against the G., H. and S. A. Railway Company and Others. SERIES NOW AGGREGATE OVFR $95,000 All Brought by Negroes Who Allege that They Were Mistreated on One of the Company's Train.
Two more damage suits were filed in the civil district courts of this county yesterday against the Galveston, Harrisburg and San Antonio Railway company and J. B. and William Wheat. The suits are each for $20,000—one brought by Joseph Parker and the other by Richard Jones, both colored.

The petition of Parker alleges that he is a citizen of Houston and had been to Richmond, where he married Sally Jones. After the marriage, Parker's petition alleges, he, in company with his wife, boarded one of the defendant company's trains to come to Houston, where they intended to make their home. Parker's troubles began, the petition further alleges, when he made application to the agent at Richmond to purchase tickets necessary for his and his wife's passage to Houston. It is alleged that there were several white persons in the room set apart for colored people, and that when Parker approached the ticket window the most profane and violent language was used toward him in the presence of his wife, by the white persons, all of whom appeared to be under the influence of liquor.

The petition also alleges that when the train arrived the boisterous crowd boarded it, but instead of going to their own part of the train went into that part intended for occupancy by negroes.

It is claimed that the persons kept up a continuous flow of indecent and obscene language and that with drawn sixshooters and other weapons intimidated and terrorized the negro passengers, inflicting personal injury upon some of them. The plaintiff charges that the conductor was appealed to repeatedly to compel the rowdyism to cease. He failed to do so, but finally invited the negroes into the smoking compartment of the coach. The negroes were followed by the persons they sought to evade, and the same general behavior on the part of the latter characterized them there.

It is alleged that while the train was near Blodgett J. B. and William Wheat took the baggage and property of plaintiff Parker and wife and threw it from the train. Among the baggage was a grip belonging to Parker, which contained $200 in cash, a watch worth $50 and various other articles of certain stated values.

Jones' suit is a companion to that of Parker's and the allegations are substantially the same. These two suits aggre gating $40,000. are a result of the occurr ence on a train a few weeks ago, on account of which, it is claimed, Jim Mitchell, colored, lost his mind through the attack and assault of the parties who are made joint defendants with the railroad company. Suits amounting to $55,400 had previously been filed by the Mitchells.

More important real estate transfers were fled for record with the county clerk yesterday, among which are those of J. W. Biting, transferring lots 3 and 4 and the adjoining halves of lots 2 and 9, block 1, of the Hutcheson addition, to M. P. Geiselman for $2200, and A. C. Herndon to John G. Brown, conveying about seventy-eight acres near Harrisburg for $2700.

joseph-parker-richmond-1900-07.A2:
HEAVY DAMAGES WANTED. COLORED PEOPLE WHO HAD A LIVELY TRAIN EXPERIENCE. Two Wild and Woolly Texans Woke Up Things in a Coach of the G. H. & S. A. Railway, Occupied by Negroes.
Special to the Sunday Light.

Houston, Texas, August 4.—Damage suits aggregating $95,000 have been filed against the Galveston, Harrisburg and San Antonio Railway company and J. B. Wheat and William Wheat, the cause of action being the same in all. Joseph Parker, colored, wants $20,000 of the amount named. He alleges that he went to the depot with his bride to take the train, and he found the place full of waiters, most of them intoxicated. The two Wheats were in the party and they all boarded the train. The whites went into the car occupied by the colored people. They threw the plaintiff's hat from the train, as well as the hat of the bride; and it is alleged they took his grip, which contained $200 in cash, besides a gold watch worth $50, and threw that from the train. The colored people finally fled from the crowd. The plaintiff alleges that the conductor was appealed to for protection but that he was afraid to do anything. The plaintiff asks for $10,000 punitory and $10,000 actual damages.

Richard Jones, colored, was another passenger on this train, and he had the same kind of experience. He filed suits this afternoon against the Galveston, Harrisburg and San Antonio Railway company and J. B. and William Wheat for $20,000 damages. The another and sister of J. Mitchell, also colored, sue for $50,400 because of injuries inflicted on him by the Wheats, which they allege has caused Mitchell to become insane and will probably cause his death. The Wheats are under arrest at Richmond.

sam-fields-whitehall-1900-08-22.A1:
LYNCHED IN LOUSIANA.
New-Orleans, Aug. 21 (Special).—News has just reached this city of a lynching at Island, La., an out of the way corner of Livingstone Parish. The news came by a little steamer to Manchac, and thence by railroad, and few details can be obtained. The negro, Samuel Fields, entered the house of a farmer in the parish and attacked a white woman who was alone in the building. She made a desperate struggle and held the negro at bay until assistance arrived. The negro took to the swamp, but was overtaken in the neighborhood of Old River Bridge and was shot to death without the formality of the accustomed rope. His body was thrown into the river.

He Was Accused of Attempting to Assault a White Woman.
NEW ORLEANS, La., Aug. 23.—Sam Fields, a young negro, was shot to death by a mob of white men last night near White Hall, in Livingston parish. Fields had attempted an assault on Mrs. Peter Poche. He was being taken by officers to the county seat at Somerville, when the mob surrounded the buggy in which he was, took him forcibly from the officers and shot him to death. The parish is entirely quiet to-day.
